pr_title: [DRAFT, pending on alternative #14193 and #14219] Allow 'openssl enc' and 'openssl dgst' to use "unknown" ciphers and digests
pr_body:
'openssl enc' and 'openssl dgst' use opt_md() and opt_cipher() to get
the algorithms the user asks for, which only used EVP_get_cipherbyname()
and EVP_get_digestbyname().  That would only return legacy implementations
for things the libcrypto has prior knowledge of.

To allow all provider backed algorithms to be fully used, even without
libcrypto's prior knowledge, opt_md() and opt_cipher() now also use
EVP_MD_fetch() and EVP_CIPHER_fetch(), and return them in a second
pointer that our apps has to free.  This is made in such a way that
the application can otherwise continue to use the constant EVP_MD and
EVP_CIPHER pointers.

As a discussion point, this reiterates that application must know what
they have fetched explicitly, and therefore must also free (with
EVP_MD_free() or EVP_CIPHER_free() in this case), and what they have
not (which includes all constant pointers they get from all sorts of
other functions, such as EVP_MD_CTX_md()), and therefore must NOT free.

Fixes #14178
Fixes #14179

Sorry, I was wrong. Yes, it's a reasonable approach.

I think this sets a bad precedent for downstream users, requiring them to complicate their code more than is really necessary. OpenSSL is already complicated, and requiring developers to track lifetimes, as opposed to adding some code to OpenSSL to make it not necessary, is the wrong trade-off in my view.  "Will nobody think of the users?" :)

> I think this sets a bad precedent for downstream users, requiring them to complicate their code more than is really necessary.

It's actually not that complicated, it's a very simple "rule": if you fetch something explicitly, you must free it.  If you don't, you don't have to.  It does means that you have to keep track of the fetched pointers.

Do note that this is in the original design, and a lot of code in the library goes with that assumption.

The complicating factor is when the application mixes two paradigms, which our app does.

> "Will nobody think of the users?" :)

Oh I do, and I for one do *not* want to add fragility and corner cases that the users can't control into the library.

issue_context.title: [master] 'openssl dgst' can't access digests that libcrypto doesn't know about
issue_context.body:
I played a bit with external providers that offer digests that libcrypto doesn't know about, and that fails.
This is due to opt_md() (in apps/lib/opt.c) only tries to get the cipher with EVP_get_digestbyname(), never with EVP_MD_fetch().
comments: In #14182, a few solutions were discussed, I'll repeat them here

I have tested both solutions, and I can squarely say that:

-   Solution 1 works!  I have tested it, among others with the budding GOST provider (gost-engine/engine#313)
-   Solution 2...  has problems, which aren't easy to resolve.  I'll talk more about it in the next comment.

>  have tested it, among others with the budding GOST provider

A GOST Provider!! Nice!

> > have tested it, among others with the budding GOST provider
> 
> A GOST Provider!! Nice!

Very impressive work! 
But for the testing purposes it makes sense to have both engine and provider.

So, problems with Solution 2:

We need to keep track of how the EVP_MD was created.  There are three possibilities:

1.  It's a constant from within libcrypto.  That should never be freed
2.  It was created with EVP_MD_meth_new().  This classically happens in ENGINEs, but may also be done with applications.  Everyone else should regard it a constant, just like (1), and it only needs to be freed once when not needed any more, using EVP_MD_meth_free().
3.  It was created with EVP_MD_fetch().  This is a provider backed method, and is reference counted, i.e. is *not* regarded as constant by others, and if explicitly fetched, it must also be explicitly freed using EVP_MD_free()

What I've worked out is that a flag can help determine if EVP_MD_meth_new() created the EVP_MD, and thusly if EVP_MD_meth_free() should be allowed to free it.
Likewise, we can use the OSSL_PROVIDER pointer in the EVP_MD to determine if EVP_MD_free() is allowed to free it (EVP_MD_free() is a *new* function, so it can be relatively safe to say that it should only free provider backed EVP_MDs).

You all with me so far?  Ok, so let's look at this line:

https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/9dc9c7f2d7f25e100dd7d80e9bc51e205033cd8c/apps/dgst.c#L406

One would think that this is easy, just cast the return value to `(EVP_MD *)` and be happy.  But then what?  Thing is, if *md* points at an explicitly fetched `EVP_MD`, it should free it explicitly with `EVP_MD_free()`, or we will have a leak because the refcount wasn't decremented enough.
The solution to that problem could, of course, be for `EVP_MD_CTX_md()` to increment the refcount if the `EVP_MD` returned is provider backed, i.e. view that as an explicit fetch.  However, here's the catch: older applications assume that `EVP_MD_CTX_md()` return a constant, and have therefore no `EVP_MD_free()` call.  So if they get a provider backed `EVP_MD`, that will cause them to leak.
We could also continue to have `EVP_MD_CTX_md()` just return the `EVP_MD` and assume that it's going to be treated as a constant.  However, if the application does a naïve `md = (EVP_MD *)EVP_MD_CTX_md()` and later on calls `EVP_MD_free(md)`, that will lead to a double free.

This is a bad case of catch-22 with Solution 2.

From this experience, I would say that it's still better to go for solution 1, and require that applications keep track of what they fetch explicitly and what they don't, to avoid getting tangled in an impossible or *very* delicate situation.

> But for the testing purposes it makes sense to have both engine and provider.

Yes, and as you can see, that PR does exactly that.
But, let's not derail this issue, yeah?
I disagree with your catch-22 reasoning (if only because a flag can be three-way), but since you already did something in #14194 it's not worth spending time discussing.

Well, I actually tried...  and got into double free errors, or a memleak, all depending on having or not having an EVP_MD_free() at the end.  Whatever you do that's *uniform* (i.e. not having to have to variables for distinction), it risks crashing or having your sanitizer scream (and oh boy is it loud...).

So yeah, if someone can *actually* work, without having fragile corner cases, I'm ready to listen.  In the mean time, the *experience* I gained within an hour wasn't very encouraging.

@levitte - the only sane way how the md returned from EVP_MD_CTX_md(tctx) could be handled is to have the returned md as const and treat it as if the call is EVP_MD_CTX_get0_md(). So yeah you really cannot mix md returned from EVP_MD_CTX_md with md returned from explicit fetch.

Yeah, previously all md objects were basically treated like const (ignoring the EVP_MD_meth_new() case) so the md returned from EVP_getdigestbyname() and EVP_MD_CTX_md() could be treated the same. If we introduced the flag you could simplify your app by calling EVP_MD_free() on md returned from the EVP_getdigestbyname() but never on a md returned from EVP_MD_CTX_md(), that would have to be handled separately.
Is the "catch-22" issue only for MessageDigest, or does it also happen for ciphers?

> Is the "catch-22" issue only for MessageDigest, or does it also happen for ciphers?

Essentially, it comes down to a base principle related to explicit fetches.  Any application (or library for that matter) that does an *explicit fetch* must also do an *explicit free* of that pointer.  `foo = EVP_MD_fetch()` is an explicit fetch, `foo = EVP_get_digestbyname()` or `foo = EVP_MD_CTX_md()` are not.

So what this essentially boils down to is that applications (or libraries for that matter) *must* keep track of their fetched pointers, and free those at some point, but *only* those.  Applications that mix in engines need to handle the fact that methods coming from engines (for example, through a call of `EVP_get_digestbyname()`) must *not* be freed.  The easiest way to handle the combination is to do this for engine methods (i.e. the old way):

``` C
    const EVP_MD *md = EVP_get_digestbyname("whatever");
```

and do this when fetching:

``` C
    EVP_MD *fetched_md;
    const EVP_MD *md = fetched_md = EVP_MD_fetch("whatever");
```

In both cases, `md` can be used to perform the actual operations, and libcrypto will do its *implicit* fetch if it gets the pointer that came from `EVP_get_digestbyname()`.  All the application needs to add somewhere is this:

``` C
    EVP_MD_free(fetched_md);
```

In other words, `fetched_md` *only* needs to be used to keep track of explicit fetches that need to be freed.

The distinction between implicit and explicit fetches is documented, including the fact the the code doing the explicit fetch must also free it.

Please do go ahead and try.  I did yesterday, and it appears that I'm not transmitting the issues I encountered well enough.
I suggest enabling asan, that's quite enlightening.

I did this:

That looks to me like it is okay for *ciphers*.
(Also note that I made a change to `EVP_CIPHER_free`, shown in the diff.)

> Does it also hold for `EVP_CIPHER_free` ?

Yes.

The problem I found was actually with `EVP_MD_CTX_md()`, which may or may not return a provider backed EVP_MD, but that one should *not* be freed, but if you still do, there's no way for `EVP_MD_free()` to tell, so you end up with a double free.
Now, there also exists a `EVP_CIPHER_CTX_cipher()`, so the same problem applies there.

Yes, but I repeat that the md returned from EVP_MD_CTX_md() (and cipher from EVP_CIPHER_CTX_cipher()) should never be handled in the same way as those that you get from algorithm lookup (or fetch). It's practically the same as with other attributes obtained via the get0 functions. So I do not see the existence of those two functions to be a blocker for allowing EVP_MD_free() to be called on the md obtained from the algorithm lookup.

> Yes, but I repeat that the md returned from EVP_MD_CTX_md() (and cipher from EVP_CIPHER_CTX_cipher()) should never be handled in the same way as those that you get from algorithm lookup (or fetch). It's practically the same as with other attributes obtained via the get0 functions. So I do not see the existence of those two functions to be a blocker for allowing EVP_MD_free() to be called on the md obtained from the algorithm lookup.

So you still need *two* variables, one extra to hold what was returned from `EVP_MD_CTX_md()`, and some mechanism to know that this one should be used for what follows, but this one must still never be freed by the application.  May I suggest that with that idea, you study this bit of code and try to think of an elegant way to code it so the pointer from the `EVP_MD_CTX_md()` doesn't get freed?  I wasn't able to...

https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/68883d9db86534176d744c7691ac7565f5def884/apps/dgst.c#L403-L420
Well you'd still have to use another fetched_md variable to be freed here. There is no way around that.

> Well you'd still have to use another fetched_md variable to be freed here. There is no way around that.

Thank you.

The other point that I would like to make is that *a public library should **not** encourage users to try to free const things*!
That should be a core tenet in API design, and what's being proposed in #14193 goes against that.

Yes, that I completely agree with. We would have to change EVP_getdigestby... to return non-const EVP_MD. Which would be weird.
Anyway I do not want to fight for this change as I do not see the current API contract as too big issue. If new applications do not care about engines support, they are not affected by this complexity at all. And applications that want to deal with both engines and providers can handle that.
I believe this was fixed in #14135 and should be closed.
Yes, fetch is now used in both opt_cipher and opt_md.
